newsitem.title: CANADA: Antamina surpasses Rio Algom, Inmet hopes.
newsitem.headline: Antamina surpasses Rio Algom, Inmet hopes.

text.p: The Antamina copper and zinc property in Peru is surpassing the original expectations of its new owners, Canadian companies Rio Algom Ltd and Inmet Mining Corp, company officials said on Wednesday.
"Quite frankly, we don't know of any other deposits that have this kind of grade presently under development in South America," said Ulli Rath, Rio Algom's vice-president of corporate development.
The companies announced interim results of their drill program at Antamina, showing a resource of at least 400 million tonnes of 1.8 percent copper equivalent.
The results from 21,000 metres of new drilling show an average of 1.2 percent copper, 1.1 percent zinc, 13 grams per tonne of silver and 0.03 percent molybdenum.
"We're very encouraged," said Bill James, chief executive of Inmet. "This one makes Inmet. This one makes her go."

The two companies have formed a 50-50 joint venture to explore Antamina after buying rights to the site from the Peruvian state last July for US$20 million. They have committed US$2.5 billion to develop the prospect.
When the companies bought Antamina, they said they needed at least 200 million tonnes of ore to make a viable mine.
They projected production of 40,000 tonnes of ore per day.
"Clearly 40,000 tonnes a day is low," said Rath. "We see possibly 60,000 tonnes day," he said, explaining that his estimate was preliminary.
He said capital expenditures at this point look like they will total about US$1.3 billion.
The companies plan to drill another 200 holes and then proceed with a full feasibility study.
"We've come a long way from a very speculative situation to a point where the partners believe they have a project," said Rath.

Much of the drilling will focus on verifying the resource numbers and moving the resource up into the measured and indicated category, he said. Right now, 200 million tonnes fit in that category, grading 1.3 percent copper, 1.1 percent zinc, 15 grams per tonne of silver and 0.03 percent molybdenum. The companies said they will release an updated resource calculation later this year. Inmet may have to sell some of its assets to pay for its share of the development costs, James said.
"We might sell the odd thing," he said in an interview. He would not say which of the company's assets would be sold.
